steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Psychologists report that children in nine-month schools typically forget a significant amount of schooling during summer breaks.

steps.label: Conclusion (We should conclude)
steps.body: The twelve-month schedule is to be preferred insofar as academic learning is concerned.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
steps.body: [The twelve-month schedule with three month-long breaks] will insure that students will not forget their schooling during their breaks.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Line up what the psychologists studied against what the author concludes.

The research is about one schedule. Children in nine-month schools forget a significant amount during summer breaks. That's it. Nothing in the evidence is about the twelve-month schedule. Yet the author claims that schedule "will insure" students do not forget during their breaks.

Where does that guarantee come from? The author is assuming forgetting is a problem of the nine-month schedule only. But the twelve-month schedule still has breaks. Three of them, each a month long.

Given that kids forget over a long summer, how could we argue the twelve-month plan is no better? Maybe kids forget plenty in a month, too. If a month away wipes out most of what a summer away does, the twelve-month schedule could mean three rounds of forgetting instead of one.

So the gap is in the comparison. The evidence shows a bad result in one situation, says nothing about the other, and the author treats the other as free of it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the argument assumes, without evidence, that forgetting during breaks happens only under the nine-month schedule. A "fails to consider" version would also work: the argument fails to consider that students might forget during month-long breaks too. Either way, the answer should point at the missing evidence about the twelve-month schedule.

notes.body: The argument never weighs academic against nonacademic learning. It limits itself on purpose: the twelve-month schedule is preferred "insofar as academic learning is concerned." Test the presumption: if academic and nonacademic experiences were worth exactly the same, would the argument lose anything? No. It needs no view about their comparative worth.

The two groups here, children on a nine-month schedule and children on a twelve-month schedule, differ in exactly the way the argument cares about: how the breaks are arranged. That distinction is the subject of the argument, not an arbitrary line. The problem is what the author assumes about one side, not where the line is drawn.

This matches the prediction in formal words. The "two situations" are the two schedules. The "undesirable result" is forgetting schooling over a break. The evidence ties that result to the nine-month schedule, and the author takes for granted that it belongs to that schedule alone, so the month-long breaks are assumed to be safe.

When a comparison has evidence about only one option, check whether the argument quietly assumes the other option is free of the problem. That unstated "only" is what an answer like this one names.

Questioning the sample attacks the one part of the argument that has evidence behind it. The research only needs to describe children in nine-month schools, and nothing suggests it doesn't. Grant that the data is perfectly representative and the argument still fails, because no one has shown that month-long breaks avoid the same forgetting.

The author accepts the psychologists' finding and uses it as the main evidence. That view is never rejected later in the argument. If anything, the argument leans on the research too far, by stretching a finding about summer breaks into a promise about month-long breaks.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Psychologists report that children in nine-month schools typically forget a significant amount of schooling during summer breaks.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (We should conclude)
old_steps.body: The twelve-month schedule is to be preferred insofar as academic learning is concerned.

old_steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
old_steps.body: [The twelve-month schedule with three month-long breaks] will insure that students will not forget their schooling during their breaks.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: This argument compares one plan [12-month schedule] to another [9-month schedule] and states that the 12-month schedule is preferable. We should consider factors that might have been left out of this comparison. For example, what if a longer, 12-month schedule with three month-long breaks will somehow make students even more forgetful? The argument claims that the 12-month schedule "will insure" that students will not forget their schooling during breaks. But that's a prediction about the future. That's what makes it an intermediate conclusion, not just a premise. It's a claim that might or might not be true. The conclusion is about "academic learning," not just remembering or forgetting. Could the 12-month plan have some unintended negative consequences that would make it worse for learning overall, even if it was better for retention? Comparative arguments frequently overlook these types of potential objections. They'll tell us that one of two options has a certain good quality. Based on that, they'll conclude that this option is better overall. It's a classic example of an "incomplete comparison."

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: A correct answer might describe an objection like the ones we've considered here, pointing out that the argument has "failed to consider" or "overlooked" this possible objection. Beware of answers that describe something which isn't actually happening in the argument, even if it seems related at first glance.

old_notes.body: The argument's assumptions are about whether students will forget schooling during breaks, not about the comparative value of academic vs. nonacademic learning. The argument explicitly states its conclusion applies "insofar as academic learning is concerned," so it is already limiting itself to academic considerations. An assumption about the relative worth of academic and nonacademic experiences is not what makes this argument vulnerable.

This answer describes an arbitrary distinction between two groups. But the argument compares two scheduling plans, not two groups of students. No actual group of twelve-month-schedule students is mentioned — the argument is making predictions about a proposed schedule. Furthermore, the distinction between the two schedules (nine months with summer vs. twelve months with shorter breaks) is not "arbitrary" — it is the substantive basis for the comparison. The argument's flaw is not that it makes an arbitrary distinction but that it assumes an unproven advantage for one of the compared options.

This precisely describes the argument's flaw. The argument identifies an undesirable result — students forgetting their schooling during breaks — and presents evidence that this result occurs in the nine-month schedule. It then assumes this result is correlated only with the nine-month schedule, concluding that the twelve-month schedule will prevent forgetting. But no evidence is offered about whether students in twelve-month programs also forget during their month-long breaks. The argument "takes for granted" that the negative outcome is unique to one option when it could easily affect both. This is the incomplete-comparison flaw at the heart of the argument.

This answer suggests the data on nine-month schools might not be representative of children generally. But the argument does not need the data to be representative of all children — it only needs the data to be accurate about children in nine-month schools, which is what the psychologists studied. Furthermore, the argument's flaw is not about the quality of the evidence about nine-month schools; it is about the absence of evidence about twelve-month schools. The data could be perfectly representative, and the argument would still be flawed for assuming the twelve-month schedule avoids the forgetting problem.

This answer describes a self-contradiction flaw: accepting a view and then rejecting it. No such contradiction exists in this argument. The argument presents the psychologists' finding about nine-month schools and uses it as evidence — it never rejects or contradicts it. The argument consistently treats the finding as reliable and builds upon it. If anything, the problem is that the argument over-relies on the finding by applying it selectively to one schedule while assuming the other is immune.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Making vagrancy illegal means transforming many innocuous everyday occurrences into crimes.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Vagrancy laws increase crime while purporting to reduce it.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Watch the word "crime" change jobs between the evidence and the conclusion.

The evidence is about classification. Vagrancy laws turn "innocuous everyday occurrences" into crimes. Acts that were legal yesterday are illegal today.

The conclusion is about amount. Vagrancy laws "increase crime." The columnist sets this against the laws' purpose of reducing "criminal activity," which makes it sound like people are now doing more harmful things.

Picture a park where twenty people nap on benches every week. A vagrancy law passes. The same twenty people nap on the same benches. On paper, the town now has twenty crimes a week that it didn't have before. Has anyone's behavior changed? No. The count went up because the label changed.

So the evidence supports only "more acts are now called crimes." The conclusion needs "people are committing more crime." The columnist slides from one claim to the other as if they were the same.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the argument confuses relabeling acts as crimes with an actual increase in criminal activity. It might say the argument fails to distinguish the two, or that it uses "crime" in two different senses.

notes.body: The columnist calls these occurrences "innocuous," which means harmless. The whole complaint is that harmless acts get treated as crimes. So the argument presumes the opposite of this answer: it treats the occurrences as not harmful.

The columnist never says vagrancy laws produce more innocuous occurrences. The occurrences stay the same; only their legal status changes. This answer invents an increase in the occurrences and then criticizes a causal inference the argument never makes.

Ask whether naming the occurrences would fix anything. Suppose the columnist listed them: napping on a bench, standing on a corner. The argument would still slide from "more acts count as crimes" to "more criminal activity." The vagueness isn't what breaks the argument.

On a "fails to consider" answer, ask whether the idea would weaken. Suppose crime would rise even without vagrancy laws. That says nothing about whether the laws themselves add to the count, which is the columnist's claim. Other causes of crime leave the argument untouched.

This names the slide we predicted. "An increase in criminal activity" is what the conclusion claims. "The reclassification of certain occurrences as crimes" is all the evidence shows.

When a conclusion reuses a word from the evidence, check whether the word means the same thing in both places. If it doesn't, the right answer says the argument fails to distinguish the two meanings, just as this one does.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Making vagrancy illegal means transforming many innocuous everyday occurrences into crimes.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: Vagrancy laws increase crime while purporting to reduce it.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: The argument presents evidence about "transforming many innocuous everyday occurrences into crimes" and then makes a leap to a new concept in the conclusion—increasing crime. The argument doesn't clearly explain what "increase crime" is intended to mean. It's reasonable to think this means that entirely new crimes take place, ones that did not occur before the vagrancy laws were passed. For example, in a certain town there might be 10 cases a month where someone actually trespasses on another person's property, but once vagrancy laws are passed that number jumps to 30 actual instances of trespassing. However, the evidence suggests that something different could be happening. It suggests that actions which were not illegal become illegal once vagrancy laws are passed. This could mean, for example, that napping under a tree in a public park is legal until vagrancy laws make it illegal. The actual number of people who nap under trees might stay exactly the same, or even decrease, but because it is now a crime, there is a sudden increase in the number of people who are arrested or fined for it. The argument doesn't clearly explain the link between innocuous occurrences becoming crimes and an increase in crime. It's not clear what "increase" actually means in this conclusion.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: A correct answer might point out how the phrase "increase crime" is used in an unclear way. It might point out that the argument doesn't establish a clear link between innocuous occurrences becoming crimes and an actual increase in crime.

old_notes.body: The argument calls these everyday occurrences "innocuous," suggesting they are not harmful. It does not presume they are harmful to society — it says the opposite.

The argument does not claim there is an increase in innocuous everyday occurrences. It says those occurrences are reclassified as crimes. The occurrences themselves may not increase at all — they simply receive a new legal classification. This answer mischaracterizes the evidence.

The argument does not need to specify what the innocuous occurrences are. The flaw would exist regardless of whether examples were provided. Even if the argument named specific behaviors, it would still conflate reclassification with an actual increase in criminal activity.

Whether crime would increase without vagrancy laws is irrelevant to the argument's flaw. The argument focuses on what happens when vagrancy laws are enacted. External factors affecting crime rates independently of vagrancy laws do not address the internal logical problem of conflating reclassification with an actual increase in crime.

This answer identifies the argument's core flaw. The argument uses "increase crime" in the conclusion without distinguishing between two very different meanings: (1) an actual increase in harmful criminal activity, and (2) the reclassification of previously legal behaviors as crimes. The evidence supports only meaning (2) — more things are now labeled as crimes — but the conclusion seems to claim meaning (1) — that there is more actual criminal activity. By failing to make this distinction, the argument equivocates on what "increase crime" means.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The best seafood gumbo requires fresh okra.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: If this claim were true [Chris's okra supplier cannot reliably supply fresh okra], then Chris's customers could not count on getting good seafood gumbo.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The evidence is a conditional. Fresh okra is required for the best seafood gumbo:

best gumbo → fresh okra

Its contrapositive tells us what happens without fresh okra:

no fresh okra → no best gumbo

That's what the evidence supports. Now read the conclusion closely. Without reliable fresh okra, customers could not count on good gumbo:

no fresh okra → no good gumbo

"Best" became "good." Those are different standards. A gumbo can be good without being the best. Without fresh okra, Chris might still serve a very good gumbo that just isn't the best one possible.

So the critic takes a requirement for the top level of quality and treats it as a requirement for a merely good level. Given the evidence, how could we argue customers can still count on good gumbo? Say good gumbo doesn't need fresh okra at all.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the argument assumes that whatever the best seafood gumbo requires, good seafood gumbo also requires. It might also say the argument fails to consider that good gumbo could be made without fresh okra.

notes.body: The critic never relies on the competitor being right. The argument only says what would follow "If this claim were true." A biased source can still make a claim, and a hypothetical about that claim stands or falls on its own logic. The bias never touches the reasoning.

This describes a quality passing from an ingredient to the dish: stale okra, so stale gumbo. The critic does something different. The okra lacks freshness, and the critic concludes the gumbo lacks goodness. Those are two different qualities, so this isn't the error. The real error is the shift from "best" to "good."

This is the tempting one, because it uses necessary and sufficient language and mentions both "best" and "good." Check what the argument does with fresh okra. It treats fresh okra as required for good gumbo: no fresh okra, no good gumbo. That's treating it as necessary, not sufficient.

To confuse it with a sufficient condition, the critic would have to argue that fresh okra guarantees good gumbo. The critic never says that. The error is a necessary condition moved from one standard to another, not a necessary condition flipped into a sufficient one.

This matches the prediction. The evidence says fresh okra is necessary for the best seafood gumbo. The conclusion uses fresh okra as if it were necessary for good seafood gumbo.

When a conclusion leans on a requirement from the evidence, check that the requirement is attached to the same thing. Here it moved from "best" to "good," and that move is the flaw this answer describes.

The critic's hypothetical already allows for this. A supplier who "cannot reliably supply" fresh okra may still deliver it on some days, and customers still couldn't count on getting it. Considering the possibility changes nothing, and it never touches the jump from "best" to "good."

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: The best seafood gumbo requires fresh okra.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: If this claim were true [Chris's okra supplier cannot reliably supply fresh okra], then Chris's customers could not count on getting good seafood gumbo.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: The evidence is a conditional statement: `best gumbo → fresh okra`. Using the contrapositive, we can conclude that if we don't have fresh okra, we cannot have the best seafood gumbo: `~ fresh okra → ~ best gumbo`. The argument tries to make a very similar conclusion, but there is an important term shift. The conclusion of this argument is about getting good gumbo, not the best gumbo: `~ fresh okra → ~ good gumbo`. It might be possible to make good seafood gumbo without fresh okra, just not the best seafood gumbo.

old_notes.body: The conclusion is conditional: if the claim is true, then the consequence follows. The argument does not assume the competitor's claim is true. It evaluates what would happen if the claim were true, which avoids the bias concern.

This would apply if the argument claimed the gumbo is not fresh because the okra is not fresh. But the argument is about quality levels — best versus good — not about transferring a quality from ingredient to dish.

This claims fresh okra is treated as sufficient for good gumbo. But the argument does not conclude that having fresh okra guarantees good gumbo. It concludes that lacking fresh okra prevents good gumbo. The actual flaw is conflating what is necessary for the best gumbo with what is necessary for good gumbo.

The evidence establishes fresh okra as a necessary ingredient for the best seafood gumbo. The conclusion assumes fresh okra is also necessary for good gumbo. But the best and good are different quality thresholds. Good gumbo might be achievable without fresh okra — you just cannot make the best gumbo. This answer precisely identifies the unjustified assumption that what is necessary for the highest quality is also necessary for adequate quality.

Even if Chris occasionally gets fresh okra, the conclusion is about customers being able to count on good gumbo reliably. Occasional availability does not address the reliability concern or the best-versus-good distinction that is the actual flaw.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: People can either fight for anarchy or they can tolerate totalitarian government control. History shows that government control of all facets of human life destroys the spirit, making life miserable. Anarchy allows each individual the freedom to pursue a personal course of happiness.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: People should fight for anarchy.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with the first sentence, because the whole argument rests on it: people "can either fight for anarchy or they can tolerate totalitarian government control."

Those are the two extremes. Anarchy means no government at all. Totalitarian control means government controls "all facets of human life." What about everything in between? A government that runs the courts and the roads but leaves your personal life alone is neither one.

Now look at the support. The evidence attacks only total control: it destroys the spirit and makes life miserable. Fine. Given that, how could we still argue against fighting for anarchy? Point to a third option. If limited government is available, rejecting totalitarian control doesn't push us to anarchy. It could just as easily push us to the middle.

The argument works only if those two options are the only ones. That's a false choice: two options presented as if nothing else exists.

Notice the flaw sits in a premise. We usually accept premises as true, but when an argument reaches its conclusion by knocking out one side of an either/or, the right answer can point out that the either/or was never complete.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the argument treats anarchy and totalitarian control as the only two options, or that it fails to consider some form of government between the two.

notes.body: The argument does give a reason anarchy beats total control. Total control "destroys the spirit," while anarchy "allows each individual the freedom to pursue a personal course of happiness." So the claim that the argument makes no attempt to explain this is false. The answer misdescribes the argument.

The argument names tolerating totalitarian control as an option and then recommends against it. Naming an option is not endorsing it. Nowhere does the anarchist say people should tolerate totalitarian government, so there is no contradiction.

This reverses the direction. The evidence is that totalitarian control makes life miserable, and the conclusion is that people should fight for anarchy. Check any "infers X from Y" answer: Y must match the evidence and X the conclusion. Here they are swapped.

The anarchist says "history shows" that total control destroys the spirit. That is an indication of evidence, even if the details aren't given. This answer says there is no indication at all, which the text contradicts.

This is the false choice. The first sentence offers only two paths, and the argument needs that to be true: rejecting one path proves the other only when nothing else is available.

When an argument gets to its conclusion by eliminating one option, check whether it has shown the options were the only ones. If it hasn't, an answer like this one names the flaw.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: People can either fight for anarchy or they can tolerate totalitarian government control. History shows that government control of all facets of human life destroys the spirit, making life miserable. Anarchy allows each individual the freedom to pursue a personal course of happiness.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: People should fight for anarchy.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: "Should" tends to be a strong word on the LSAT. When the conclusion of an argument makes a recommendation, stating what someone "should" do, the evidence is supposed to clearly justify why that is the best course of action. As a general rule, we accept the evidence that we're given in LR questions. However, difficult LR questions will occasionally test our critical thinking skills in a more holistic way. To answer these questions correctly, we need to be flexible and take a big-picture view, rather than mechanically following general rules. Even though we can consider the first sentence of this argument as evidence, it stands out as rather extreme statement. Anarchy and totalitarian government control are extremes at the opposite ends of the spectrum. Most systems of government that exist fall somewhere in between. Is it reasonable to think that anarchy and totalitarian government control are the only two options available? No, it's not. There is a clear false choice flaw baked into this premise, which makes the argument questionable from the start.

old_notes.body: The argument does explain why anarchy is desirable — it allows freedom to pursue happiness. And it explains why totalitarianism is undesirable — it destroys the spirit. This answer mischaracterizes the argument.

The argument does not say people should tolerate totalitarianism — it argues they should fight for anarchy instead. The first sentence presents toleration as one option; the conclusion recommends against it. There is no contradiction within the argument.

This answer reverses the argument's actual logic. The argument infers from "totalitarianism is objectionable" that "people should fight for anarchy" — not the other way around. This answer has the direction of inference backwards.
The argument says "history shows" that totalitarianism makes life miserable. "History" is offered as evidence. This answer claims no evidence is indicated, which contradicts the text.

This identifies the false dichotomy. The argument presents only two options — anarchy and totalitarianism — as if nothing exists between them. In reality, most political systems occupy the vast middle ground: democracies, republics, constitutional monarchies, and numerous other forms of limited government. By excluding these alternatives, the argument artificially narrows the choice to make anarchy seem like the only reasonable option.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Many of the words used to describe web sites evoke ideas that are usually associated with real estate. The common law of trespass usually applies to cases of encroachment on real estate.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: It is reasonable to extend that law [trespass] to protect against encroachments on property in cyberspace.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The evidence is about words. We call a web page a "site," and we talk about "visiting" it. Those words also describe land.

The conclusion is about law. Trespass law, which protects land, should be extended to protect property in cyberspace.

The bridge between them is an analogy: web sites resemble real estate, so they should be treated like real estate. But what resemblance has been shown? Only that we use some of the same words. That's a similarity in vocabulary, not in anything that matters to the law.

Test it with another shared word. We "drive" traffic to a web page. Should traffic laws apply to web pages? Of course not. Shared vocabulary doesn't show that two things are alike in the ways a law cares about, such as how they can be entered, damaged, or used without permission.

Given the evidence, how could we argue against the conclusion? Point out that a web site might share nothing with land except the words we use for it.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the analogy between web sites and real estate rests only on shared words. A "fails to show" version works too: the argument fails to show the two are alike in any way that matters for trespass law.

notes.body: The argument never claims that people consider cyberspace property to be real estate. It claims only that some words for web sites "evoke ideas" of real estate. And even if many people did consider it real estate, that would be one more fact about how we talk and think, not a reason the law should treat the two alike.

Circular reasoning needs a premise that already assumes the conclusion. Check the premises: some words for web sites evoke real estate, and trespass law usually applies to real estate. Neither says trespass law should cover cyberspace. The conclusion goes beyond them, which is the opposite of circular.

The tempting part is the first sentence: most lawyers think copyright law is the best protection for web site owners. But that isn't evidence against extending trespass law. Copyright law could be the best tool while trespass law is still a reasonable addition. The evidence gives weak support for the conclusion, not support for the opposite.

This matches the prediction. The "similarities that constitute the analogy" are the shared words "site" and "visiting," and "merely verbal" names exactly what's wrong with them.

When an argument concludes that two things should be treated alike, ask what similarity it has actually shown, and whether that similarity matters for the treatment it recommends. Here the only similarity is in vocabulary.

The argument mentions expert opinion only to move away from it. Most lawyers favor copyright law, and the argument ends up recommending trespass law. It never defends its view by pointing to what experts believe.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Many of the words used to describe web sites evoke ideas that are usually associated with real estate. The common law of trespass usually applies to cases of encroachment on real estate.

old_steps.label: Conclusion
old_steps.body: It is reasonable to extend that law [trespass] to protect against encroachments on property in cyberspace.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: The evidence notes a similarity between web sites and real estate. Many of the same words, like "site" and "visiting" are used when discussing both web sites and real estate. But then the argument gets cheeky. It uses this one similarity, which is pretty superficial, as a basis for claiming that web sites and real estate are similar in another way: the same types of laws should apply to both. When two types of activities happen to use similar terminology, does that necessarily mean that the same types of laws should apply to both? If I drive a car and also use Google Drive on my computer, do I have to obey local traffic laws while sitting at my desk using my laptop? If so, I guess I should put on a seatbelt and get rid of this glass of wine...

old_notes.body: The argument does not claim cyberspace property is "widely considered to be real estate." It draws an analogy based on shared terminology. This answer addresses a stronger claim than the argument makes.

No premise presupposes the conclusion. The premises about shared terminology and trespass law's real estate application are factual claims independent of whether trespass law should apply to cyberspace. The flaw is a weak analogy, not circular logic.

The evidence does not contradict the conclusion — it is just weak. Shared terminology provides some minimal support for the legal analogy, not evidence against it. The problem is insufficiency, not self-contradiction.

This precisely identifies the flaw. The argument's analogy between web sites and real estate rests entirely on shared vocabulary. No evidence is provided that web sites and real estate share substantive characteristics relevant to legal treatment — such as exclusive possession, physical boundaries, or interference with use. The answer correctly states that the argument fails to show the similarities go beyond verbal coincidence.

The argument challenges the lawyers' view (copyright law) in favor of trespass law. It does not defer to expert opinion — it contradicts it. This answer reverses the argument's relationship to authority.

steps.label: Conclusion (This indicates that)
steps.body: Swahili culture was to some extent influenced by Oromo culture.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: In the 14th and 15th centuries, the Swahilis built tombs with big pillars and paneled outsides. Those types of tombs are also super common among the Oromo, who were in contact with Swahili. But no other culture known to have mixed with the Swahili has these types of tombs.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with the curious fact. The Swahili and the Oromo both built tombs with large pillars and paneled facades, and no other people in contact with the Swahili built them.

The historian's explanation: Oromo culture influenced Swahili culture. That's a claim about direction. The style traveled from the Oromo to the Swahili.

What evidence points that way? None. The evidence shows the two cultures share the style. It dates the Swahili tombs to the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, but gives no date at all for the Oromo ones.

Given that, how could we argue the Swahili were not influenced by the Oromo? Flip the arrow. Maybe the Swahili built these tombs first and the Oromo picked up the style from them. Everything in the evidence fits that story just as well. (The two cultures could even have arrived at the style independently.)

For the Oromo to have influenced the Swahili, the Oromo must have had the style first. The historian takes that for granted.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the historian assumes the Oromo built these tombs before the Swahili did. A "fails to consider" version works too: the argument fails to consider that the Swahili may have influenced the Oromo.

notes.body: The historian's point is about a building style: large pillars and paneled facades. Suppose the Oromo used these structures for something other than tombs. The style could still have passed from one culture to the other. What the buildings were used for doesn't touch the question of who influenced whom.

This flaw needs a timeline: A came before B, so A caused B. The historian gives no such timeline. There's a date for the Swahili tombs and nothing for the Oromo ones. The real trouble runs the other way: the argument needs the Oromo to come first and never shows it.

Drawing a narrower conclusion than your evidence allows is caution, not a flaw. And the premises don't strongly support anything broader than influence "to some extent." The trouble is the direction of the influence, not its size.

This sounds like the classic alternative-explanation answer, so test it. "Takes for granted" means ask whether the argument needs it. Suppose a third civilization did create the first such tombs, passed the style to the Oromo, and the Oromo passed it to the Swahili. The conclusion still holds: Swahili culture was influenced by Oromo culture. The argument doesn't need to rule out a third civilization, so it doesn't assume one away.

This is the prediction. Influence runs in a direction, and the conclusion picks one: Oromo to Swahili. That requires the Oromo to have built these tombs first, and the historian offers nothing about when the Oromo built them.

Whenever a conclusion says one group influenced another, ask what establishes the order. If nothing does, the assumption that the source came first is the gap.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (This indicates that)
old_steps.body: Swahili culture was to some extent influenced by Oromo culture.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: In the 14th and 15th centuries, the Swahilis built tombs with big pillars and paneled outsides. Those types of tombs are also super common among the Oromo, who were in contact with Swahili. But no other culture known to have mixed with the Swahili has these types of tombs.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: There is a curious fact — how come both the Oromo and the Swahili both have this style of tomb? The author's causal explanation is that the Oromo invented that style and then influenced the Swahili, who 'copied' that style. We can object that the author is being overconfident in settling on that causal storyline, when there could be other ways to explain it. Maybe the Swahili invented the style and the Oromo copied it from them. Normally, we'd say, "maybe they both copied it from some 3rd culture", but it says that no other culture the Swahili was in contact with had this style of tomb. It could be that both cultures just happened to coincidentally start the same style, without being influenced by each other.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: The answer will deal with an Alternate Explanation for how Oromo and Swahili both ended up with that distinctive style of tomb, or it will deal with the plausibility of the author's story that the Oromo created the style and then influenced Swahili culture to use the same style.

old_notes.body: This answer suggests the Oromo might not have used the structures as tombs. But the argument's claim is about architectural influence, not about the specific function of the structures. Even if the Oromo used pillar-and-panel structures for different purposes, the architectural similarity still suggests cultural contact and potential influence. The historian's conclusion is about the transmission of an architectural style, and the specific use to which the structures were put does not affect whether the style was shared and who influenced whom. The real flaw is about directionality, not about functional differences.

This answer describes a post hoc ergo propter hoc flaw — concluding that because one event preceded another, the first caused the second. But the historian's argument does not establish any temporal sequence. The historian never claims the Oromo had the structures before the Swahili. In fact, the absence of temporal evidence is precisely the flaw — the historian assumes a direction of influence without establishing chronological priority. This answer describes a flaw that would require the historian to have claimed chronological precedence, which the historian did not. The actual flaw is the failure to consider that the chronological relationship might run in the opposite direction.

Drawing a restricted conclusion from strong premises is not a flaw — it is actually a logical virtue. If the premises strongly support a broader conclusion and the argument draws a narrower one, the argument is being appropriately cautious. The historian's conclusion includes the hedge "to some extent," which is indeed a restricted claim. But being cautious is not a logical error. The problem with the argument is not that the conclusion is too narrow — it is that the direction of influence is assumed without evidence. This answer describes something praiseworthy about the argument's structure rather than identifying its actual weakness.

This answer suggests the argument should have considered whether a third civilization created the original structures. While this is a conceivable alternative explanation, it is less central than the primary flaw. The historian already noted that these structures "are unknown among any other people with whom the Swahili civilization had contact," which partially addresses the third-party concern for known contacts. The more fundamental flaw is simpler: even if only two groups are involved, the argument fails to establish which one influenced the other. The direction of influence between the two known groups is the critical unaddressed question, not the existence of an unknown third party.

This answer identifies the argument's central flaw: the historian assumes the Oromo had these structures before the Swahili did, without providing any evidence for that temporal ordering. The argument establishes that both groups share a distinctive architectural feature not found among other Swahili contacts. This supports the inference that influence occurred between the two groups. But influence is directional, and the shared feature alone does not indicate which direction. The Swahili could have developed the style first and transmitted it to the Oromo. By concluding that "Swahili culture was influenced by Oromo culture," the historian assumes the Oromo had temporal priority — a claim the evidence does not establish. Without knowing who built the structures first, the argument cannot determine the direction of influence.

steps.label: Conclusion (Hence)
steps.body: There are celestial objects in this galaxy that generate light but are not stars.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Stars generate light. Planets do not generate light. There are many other celestial objects in this galaxy that are not planets.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Sort the celestial objects in this galaxy into three groups. Stars generate light. Planets don't; they only reflect it. And there are "many other celestial objects" that are neither.

The conclusion says some of those other objects generate light. Why? The evidence never says whether the other objects generate light. The author seems to reason: planets don't generate light, these objects aren't planets, so some of them do. Here is the shape:

planet → does not generate light
some objects are not planets
so, some of those objects generate light

That's an illegal negation. The rule tells us what is true of something that is a planet. It tells us nothing about things that aren't planets. The author is treating planets as if they were the only objects that don't generate light, and nothing supports that.

Given the evidence, how could we argue the conclusion is false? Suppose every one of those other objects is dark, like a planet. Then there are many objects that are neither stars nor planets, and none of them generates light.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The stem says "fails to consider," so look for a possibility that would wreck the conclusion. The best one: objects other than planets might also fail to generate light. The answer might put it exactly that way: planets are not the only objects that do not generate light.

notes.body: Run the "fails to consider" test: would this weaken? Suppose planets are the only objects that reflect light. Then the other objects don't reflect light. That still says nothing about whether they generate it; they could do neither. The gap about generating light stays exactly where it was.

The argument is only about this galaxy. Whether this galaxy holds a tiny share of the universe's objects or most of them, the question is the same: do any of its non-star, non-planet objects generate light? The size of the galaxy's share doesn't touch that.

Objects in other galaxies are outside the argument. The conclusion is about light-generating objects "in this galaxy." Knowing that some objects elsewhere generate light can't make the conclusion any more or less likely to be true here.

The argument never says light is the only difference between stars and planets. It uses light because that's what the conclusion is about. Stars and planets could differ in a hundred ways and the gap would remain: nothing shows the other objects generate light.

This names the overlooked possibility. The argument needs some of the non-planet objects to generate light, and it simply assumes they do, as if planets were the only objects that don't. Say other objects also fail to generate light, and the many non-planet objects no longer prove anything.

On a "fails to consider" answer, ask whether the idea would weaken the argument. This one opens exactly the gap the argument skipped.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (Hence)
old_steps.body: There are celestial objects in this galaxy that generate light but are not stars.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Stars generate light. Planets do not generate light. There are many other celestial objects in this galaxy that are not planets.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body:
This argument is so bad that it's hard to understand what the author is going for. She establishes a difference between stars and planets (the former generates light and the latter doesn't). Then she affirms that there are other celestial objects besides stars and planets. Then she concludes these other objects (or at least some of them) are like stars, rather than like planets, when it comes to generating light. Why? Why wouldn't we just as easily assume that the other objects are like planets and don't generate light? She seems to be assuming that planets are uniquely the celestial objects that don't generate light and that all the other celestial objects do. Her argument could be thought of as an illegal negation:
```
Planet → does not generate light
Some X's are not Planets.
Hence, Some X's do generate light.
```
She's arguing, "if there are other celestial objects that aren't planets, then there are other celestial objects that do generate light", which means she's assuming, "If it's not a planet, then it does generate light".

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: We could potentially call out this Illegal Negation with an answer saying the author is confusing a condition that's sufficient to show you don't generate light (being a planet) with one that's necessary. However, since this question stem prefaced with "fails to consider" they might weaken the Nec vs. Suff error the "conversational" way, where we object to the conditional relationship the author is imagining by saying that the Left side could be true while the Right side is false. This author is imagining that "If it's not a planet, then it generates light". So we can say she fails to consider that something could be the Left side but not the Right side (something could be "not a planet" but not be "something that generates light"). Or we could just complain that the author presents two celestial objects (stars and planets), one that does generate light and one that doesn't. Then she assumes that a 3rd category of celestial objects ("other" celestial objects) belongs in the generating light category, for no apparent reason. The author fails to consider that these other celestial objects could be more like planets than they are like stars, when it comes to light-generating properties.

old_notes.body: Whether or not there are other celestial objects that reflect light besides planets is irrelevant to the argument's flaw. The argument's error is about generating light, not reflecting it. Even if planets were the only objects that reflect light, the argument would still fail because it assumes that all non-planet, non-star objects must generate light. The distinction between reflecting and not reflecting light does not address the core gap: the argument never establishes that every non-planet object generates light. Objects that neither reflect nor generate light (like dark asteroids or dust clouds) would also undermine the conclusion, and this answer does not touch that possibility.

The percentage of celestial objects in this galaxy relative to all celestial objects everywhere is irrelevant to the argument's reasoning. The argument is about what types of objects exist in this galaxy and whether they generate light. Whether this galaxy contains 1% or 99% of all celestial objects in the universe has no bearing on whether the non-planet, non-star objects in this galaxy generate light. The flaw is entirely about the logical categories within this galaxy — specifically, the assumption that non-planet objects must generate light. Scaling the argument to the broader universe does not address this internal logical error.

Whether celestial objects outside this galaxy also generate light has no relevance to the argument's flaw. The argument concludes that there are light-generating non-stars in this galaxy. The reasoning error is the assumption that all non-planet objects in this galaxy must generate light. Objects in other galaxies — whether they generate light or not — do not affect this internal logical gap. The argument could be perfectly correct or perfectly flawed about this galaxy regardless of what happens in distant galaxies. The flaw is about how categories of objects are classified within the argument's own scope.

The argument never claims that the only difference between stars and planets is light generation. The argument's reasoning depends on a simple chain: planets do not generate light, other non-planet objects exist, therefore those other objects generate light. The number of features distinguishing stars from planets is irrelevant to this chain. Even if there are a hundred differences between stars and planets, the argument's flaw remains: it assumes that all non-planet objects must generate light. Knowing that stars and planets differ in additional ways beyond light generation does not address whether that assumption is justified. The overlooked possibility is about what non-planet objects do, not about how stars and planets compare.

The argument's logical chain runs as follows: stars generate light, planets do not generate light, and there are non-star, non-planet celestial objects in this galaxy — therefore some non-star objects must generate light. This conclusion follows only if planets are the only celestial objects that do not generate light. If other non-planet objects — such as asteroids, comets, dust clouds, or dark matter — also fail to generate light, then the mere existence of non-planet objects does not establish that any of them are light-generating. The argument treated the celestial object classification as a simple three-way split: stars (generate light), planets (do not generate light), and everything else (must generate light by default). But "everything else" could easily fall into the non-light-generating camp alongside planets. This answer identifies exactly that overlooked possibility: planets might not be the only objects that fail to generate light, which would collapse the entire inference.

steps.label: Conclusion (therefore)
steps.body: The choice between seeing a specialist or a general practitioner for needed PT will not affect one's chances of major improvement.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Among patients who received less than six weeks of PT, about 31% showed major improvement, whether they were treated by a general practitioner or by a specialist. Among patients who received PT for longer, about 50% showed major improvement, again regardless of whether they were treated by a general practitioner or by a specialist.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The conclusion is about one patient's choice: picking a specialist or a general practitioner won't change your odds of major improvement. The evidence is about whole groups: across all patients, the two kinds of practitioner get the same rates.

Can equal group rates hide real differences? Try numbers. Suppose there are two kinds of injury, sprains and fractures, and each practitioner sees as many of one as the other. General practitioners get major improvement in 50% of sprains and 12% of fractures. Specialists get 12% of sprains and 50% of fractures. Both average 31%, the same figure the records show for short treatment. The records look identical.

Now you have a fracture. Does your choice matter? Very much: 50% with a specialist, 12% with a general practitioner. The equal totals hid the fact that each practitioner is better at a different injury.

So given the evidence, how could we argue the choice does matter? Point out that the overall numbers could be an average of very different results for different injuries.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer saying the argument overlooks that the two kinds of practitioner might do better with different kinds of injuries or patients. Then equal overall rates would not mean equal odds for any one patient.

notes.body: The argument never mentions "any improvement." Its evidence and its conclusion are both about major improvement. So it can't be inferring something about major improvement from facts about any improvement. This answer criticizes a step the argument never takes.

The argument doesn't need to know which injuries need short treatment and which need long. It compares the two kinds of practitioner within each length of treatment, and the rates match in both. Knowing why one injury takes six weeks and another takes longer would not reveal any difference between the practitioners.

The evidence is records of whether patients "showed major improvement." Nothing says those records come from patients rating their practitioners, so to make this answer hurt we would have to add that assumption ourselves. And a patient could feel more warmly about a specialist while the records still show the same improvement.

Percentages already account for group size. If 31% of 100 general-practitioner patients and 31% of 1,000 specialist patients improved, the rates are still equal. Unequal numbers of patients would not, by themselves, make the matching percentages misleading.

This is the hidden-subgroup problem from the numbers above. Equal overall rates can come from each kind of practitioner excelling at a different injury, and then the choice matters a lot for any one patient. On a "fails to consider" answer, ask whether the idea would weaken: here it does, because it shows equal averages can sit on top of real differences.

Whenever an argument moves from equal group results to "the choice won't matter for you," check whether the group could split into parts where the results differ.

old_steps.label: Conclusion (therefore)
old_steps.body: The choice between seeing a specialist or a general practitioner for needed PT will not affect one's chances of major improvement.

old_steps.label: Evidence
old_steps.body: Among people who received less than six weeks of PT, 31% showed major improvement, whether they were treated by a general practitioner or a by a specialist. Among people who received more PT, again about 50% showed major improvement, regardless of whether they were treated by a general practitioner or by a specialist.

old_steps.label: Evaluate
old_steps.body: This conclusion is essentially anti-causal, saying it doesn't make a difference whether you're assigned to a general practitioner or to a specialist. If we were going to argue that it does make a difference which one you're assigned to, then how are we going to explain why people seem to be getting the same rate of major improvement regardless of which type of PT they see? There is a tiny detail that crops up in the conclusion about "necessary physical therapy". The evidence didn't say that the people receiving physical therapy were getting needed physical therapy. Maybe when it's needed, it really makes a difference whether you see a GP vs. a specialist, but the records are distorted by the fact that tons of people get PT when they don't need it. Maybe we're currently doing a great job of assigning people to a GP vs. a specialist based on what their specific situation is, and if we stopped caring about which type of therapist we assigned patients, the 31% and 50% marks would go way down. Conversely, maybe we're currently not doing a great job of assigning people to a GP vs. a specialist based on their specific situation, and if we started caring about which type we assigned patients to, we would do better than 31% and 50% of patients showing major improvement.

old_steps.label: Goal
old_steps.body: The author is assuming that if both types of therapist are getting the same percent of their patients to show major improvement, then it doesn't matter whether a patient sees one or the other (for the sake of major improvement). But the author is failing to consider that those current rates of major improvement might change were we to concentrate more or concentrate less on caring about whether patients saw a specialist vs. GP based on their specific needs.

old_notes.body: The argument does not make this presumption. It never mentions patients who showed any improvement at all; its evidence and its conclusion are both about major improvement. So it cannot be inferring something about major improvement from facts about any improvement. The argument's real flaw is the failure to control for confounding variables: it does not account for differences in the types of conditions treated by specialists versus generalists. Two practitioners can show the same major-improvement rates, and the comparison can still be meaningless if they are treating fundamentally different patient populations.

Knowing which kinds of injuries require short-term versus long-term treatment is unnecessary for the argument's conclusion. The argument groups patients by duration and compares outcomes within each group. Whether back injuries need six weeks and knee injuries need twelve is irrelevant to the question of whether practitioner type affects outcomes. The argument's flaw is about who treats what types of patients, not about which injuries require which treatment durations. This answer points to missing information that would be useful for a different analysis but does not identify the logical error in the argument as presented.

Patient reporting bias — whether patients are more favorable toward one type of practitioner — is a valid methodological concern in general, but it is not the specific flaw in this argument. The argument assumes the reported improvement rates are accurate and draws a flawed conclusion from them. Even if the data is perfectly unbiased, the comparison fails because it does not control for differences in the patient populations seen by each type of practitioner. Introducing a reporting bias concern shifts attention from the argument's actual logical error (comparing non-equivalent groups) to a hypothetical data quality issue that, even if resolved, would not fix the underlying problem.

Whether the number of patients surveyed was equal between groups is not the argument's flaw. Statistical comparisons of percentages do not require equal sample sizes — the percentages are already normalized. The argument compares 31% to 31% and 50% to 50%; these percentages can be equally meaningful whether derived from 100 patients or 10,000. The flaw is that equal percentages from different patient populations are being treated as evidence of equal effectiveness. If specialists treat harder cases, equal improvement rates actually indicate superior performance by specialists. The sample size question is a statistical concern that is separate from and less fundamental than the confounding-variable problem that actually undermines the argument.

This answer identifies the argument's central flaw: it compares raw improvement rates without accounting for the possibility that specialists and generalists treat fundamentally different types of conditions. If specialists tend to handle complex, difficult cases (torn ligaments, post-surgical rehabilitation, chronic conditions) while generalists handle simpler problems (mild strains, basic mobility issues), then equal improvement rates actually indicate that specialists are more effective — they are achieving the same results with harder cases. Conversely, if generalists excel at treating certain conditions and specialists at others, a patient's choice of practitioner absolutely matters, even though the aggregate numbers look identical. The argument committed the ecological fallacy: drawing individual-level conclusions from group-level data that masks crucial subgroup differences. By overlooking that each practitioner type might have a comparative advantage with different conditions, the argument prematurely concluded that the choice does not matter.
